## Website post

# A register is a decision about who may be asked, not a list of who was admitted

Every organisation that keeps a register of counterparties ends up answering the same question twice. The first time is at admission, when a committee reads an application and decides whether the applicant belongs. The second time is at the moment of a transaction, when a clerk or a system has to decide whether the party on the other side is the party the register describes. The two answers are often assumed to be the same answer. They are not, and the distance between them is where most of the operational cost of a register lives.

Admission is a decision about membership. It is made once, on evidence gathered at a point in time, and it is recorded as a line in a list. From that moment the list is the authority. A member is a member because the list says so, and the list says so because a committee once agreed. Nothing about the transaction in front of the clerk enters into it. The register has already answered.

The transaction question is different in kind. It asks whether this signature, this message or this instruction was produced by the organisation the register names, and whether the person who produced it had the authority to do so on that day. A list cannot answer that. It can only confirm that the name exists. The gap is filled by habit, by fax headers, by phone calls to a known number and by the reasonable assumption that nobody would bother to impersonate a mid-sized firm. That assumption has held up less well each year.

The better instrument is a credential that binds the legal entity to a key and names the roles that may act for it. A credential of that kind is issued once under a governed standard, carried by the organisation, presented at the moment of the transaction and checked by the party relying on it. It can be revoked by its issuer without rewriting anyone's list. The register does not disappear; it stops being the only thing that answers the second question.

Three consequences follow for anyone who runs a register today. First, the admission process keeps its value, because the credential has to be issued to someone, and issuance is where the evidence is gathered. Second, the operational cost moves from the clerk to the issuer, which is where the evidence already sits. Third, the boundary of the register stops being the boundary of trust: a party outside the list is no longer unaddressable, only unverified until it presents a credential the relying party accepts.

None of this is a claim that lists are wrong. A list is a fine way to record a decision. The argument is narrower: a decision about who may be asked is not the same as a record of who was admitted, and a system that uses the second to answer the first will keep paying for the difference in exceptions, delays and the occasional loss. The example standards body's own report for 2026 puts the exception rate for identity queries at the top of its list of operational findings, which is the only number this piece needs.

What this piece does not say: no organisation named here operates the credential layer described, and no date is given for one. It is a specified design, and the argument stands or falls on the two questions, not on any deployment.

## LinkedIn teaser

A register answers one question at admission and is then asked a different one at every transaction.

Admission is a membership decision, made once and written as a line in a list. The transaction question asks whether this instruction came from the organisation the list names, and whether the sender had authority that day. A list confirms a name exists; it cannot confirm a signature.

The instrument that answers the second question is a credential bound to the entity, presented at the transaction and revocable by its issuer. It is a specified design, not a deployed capability, and the argument does not depend on a date.
